caption: Supernova 1987A and its ring of debris, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A ring of supernova debris glows in this Hubble Space Telescope image of SN 1987A, which lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy. Light from the exploding star reached Earth in February 1987, making it the closest supernova seen from Earth in almost 400 years.

Because it is so near, astronomers have been able to follow the explosion in detail as it changes. Hubble has kept a continuous record of SN 1987A since the telescope's launch in 1990, as part of a long-term study led by Robert Kirshner of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics.

For years the debris faded, but it has started to brighten again, which means a new power source is lighting it. The debris is beginning to strike the surrounding ring and drive powerful shock waves that produce X-rays, detected by NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory. Those X-rays light up the debris, and shock heating makes it glow in visible light. NASA describes this as an unprecedented view of a supernova turning into a supernova remnant.
explore: The brightening was reported in the journal Nature by a team that included Kirshner. Hubble's long record of the object lets astronomers compare the debris over the years, which is how the change in the power source lighting the debris was noticed.

understand.summary: A Hubble Space Telescope image. NASA has not published the filters or colour mapping for this image.
understand.eye: The colours are not documented, so they should not be read as the hues an eye would see, and the glow of the debris is lit partly by X-rays that the eye cannot see.

alt: A brightening ring of supernova debris around the site of SN 1987A.

caption: The Sombrero Galaxy (M104) in near-infrared light, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A long, brownish-yellow disk tilts across the frame from upper left to lower right, its rim edged with mottled dark brown patches. This is the Sombrero Galaxy, also called M104, in near-infrared light from the NIRCam instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope. It lies around 30 million light-years away, on the fringe of the Virgo galaxy cluster, and we see it nearly edge-on.

Dust in the outer ring blocks some light from stars inside the galaxy, but less than in Hubble's visible-light view, because longer infrared wavelengths slip past dust more easily. The huge central bulge of packed stars shines through, along with roughly 2,000 globular clusters, dense balls each holding hundreds of thousands of old stars.

The clusters hint at a turbulent past, since their stars differ chemically from one another, which a merger of galaxies over billions of years would explain. Our viewpoint sits six degrees off the galaxy's equator, and from there the inner disk looks tilted inward like the start of a funnel, a warp that also supports the merger idea.
explore: The Sombrero has a mass of about 800 billion Suns. NIRCam also picks out individual red giant stars outside the galaxy, though not necessarily at its distance. These cool stars glow brightly because of their large surface area. Background galaxies of many shapes and colours fill the rest of the field, and their colours give astronomers clues to properties such as their distance.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam took this near-infrared image. NASA shows the F090W and F200W filters in blue, F212N and F277W in green, and F335M and F444W in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and at these wavelengths the dark dust lane that dominates visible-light views is much less pronounced.

alt: An oblong brownish-yellow galaxy seen nearly edge-on, stretching from upper left to lower right, with mottled dark brown patches along the edge of its disk, against black space.

caption: Ten surveyed stars in the star cluster NGC 346, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Twisted pink and orange filaments cross a black sky scattered with white and pink stars, and ten small yellow circles mark the stars examined in a recent study. The Webb image shows the massive cluster NGC 346 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy among the Milky Way's nearest neighbours.

NGC 346 is poor in elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, much like the early universe, so it is a nearby stand-in for those conditions. Models predicted that disks around such stars would vanish too fast for big planets to grow. But in 2003 Hubble found signs of a massive planet orbiting a very old star, and in the mid 2000s it saw stars here, about 20 to 30 million years old, that apparently still kept their disks.

Webb's spectra of forming, Sun-like stars in this galaxy confirm they still have disks and are still pulling in material. The researchers suggest the disks may last longer because radiation pressure works less well with few heavy elements, or because such stars form from bigger gas clouds that build bigger disks.
explore: The cluster has only about ten percent of the heavier elements found in the Sun. Planet-forming disks in our galaxy are usually expected to disperse after 2 or 3 million years. Guido De Marchi, based at the European Space Research and Technology Centre, led the study, and the paper appeared in The Astrophysical Journal.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam captured this near-infrared view. NASA shows F444W in red, F335M in orange, F277W in cyan and F200W in blue.
understand.eye: The image records near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the yellow circles are markers added to the picture.

alt: Twisted pink and orange filaments against a black background dotted with white and pink stars, with ten small yellow circles marking individual stars.

caption: Galaxy cluster MACS J1423, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Thousands of overlapping objects fill this black field, from members of a massive galaxy cluster to distorted galaxies far behind it. The biggest bright white oval, a supergiant elliptical galaxy, is the dominant member of MACS J1423, a cluster about 5 billion light-years away in the constellation Boötes. Webb's NIRCam took the image in 2023.

The cluster's gravity works as a lens, magnifying and distorting light from objects well behind it. This gravitational lensing lets astronomers study distant galaxies in detail. One of them is the Firefly Sparkle, a galaxy seen as it was around 600 million years after the big bang. Stretched into a long arc, it shows 10 distinct star clusters that give off most of its light.

The Firefly Sparkle has a mass similar to what the Milky Way's might have been at the same early stage. Its clusters formed at different times, and its stars have not settled into a central bulge or a thin disk, signs that the galaxy is still assembling. Two companion galaxies sit close by and may shape how it grows.
explore: Webb surveyed the same field that Hubble imaged for its CLASH program, which used Wide Field Camera 3, and its near-infrared sharpness revealed many more galaxies in far greater detail. The observation is part of the CAnadian NIRISS Unbiased Cluster Survey (CANUCS). The Firefly Sparkle sits 6,500 light-years from its first companion and 42,000 light-years from its second.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam took this near-infrared image. NASA shows F115W and F150W in blue, F200W and F277W in green, and F356W and F444W in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colours here are hues assigned to Webb filters.

alt: Thousands of galaxies of varied sizes and colours on a black background, with a large bright white oval galaxy and distorted background galaxies.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1365 in mid-infrared light, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A huge galaxy fills the whole frame, with its spiral arms running off the lower right edge and a bright white, slightly pinkish core shaped like an elongated oval just off centre. This is NGC 1365, a double-barred spiral about 56 million light-years away in the constellation Fornax, seen by Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI).

At these wavelengths, clumps of dust and gas that absorbed the light of forming stars glow as they give it out again. That glow traces a network of cavernous bubbles and filament-like shells, carved by young stars pouring energy into the spiral arms. Webb also picks out several very bright star clusters near the core, and newly found young clusters along the outer edges of the bar where it joins the arms, which only Webb can see through the thick dust there.

NGC 1365 is one of the largest galaxies known, twice the length of the Milky Way. It is one of 19 galaxies studied by the PHANGS collaboration, which aims to learn how the birth of young stars affects the evolution of their galaxies.
explore: The images also show how the orbits of stars and gas depend on where they form, which accounts for the older clusters found outside the galaxy's inner ring of star formation. The PHANGS team has also observed its galaxies with Hubble, the Very Large Telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array. MIRI was contributed by ESA and NASA.

understand.summary: Webb's MIRI took this mid-infrared image. NASA shows F770W in blue, F1000W and F1130W in green, and F2100W in red.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is invisible to the eye. The PHANGS team says areas that are completely dark in Hubble images of these galaxies light up in detail in Webb's infrared views.

alt: A large spiral galaxy filling the frame, with arms extending off the lower right and a bright white, slightly pinkish oval core just off centre.

caption: Star cluster NGC 346 and its nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Arcs of orange and pink gas curve through the centre of the frame in a boat-like shape, and another plume of the same colours spreads outward. Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) captured NGC 346, a star cluster inside a nebula 200,000 light-years away in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a nearby dwarf galaxy.

The colours trace two kinds of hydrogen. Pink marks energized hydrogen, typically at around 10,000 °C or more. Orange marks dense, cold molecular hydrogen at around -200 °C or less, along with dust. Stars form in that colder gas and then reshape their surroundings, as their light breaks down dense clouds into ridges and glowing pillars.

The Small Magellanic Cloud holds fewer elements heavier than hydrogen and helium than our galaxy does, so scientists expected little dust there. Webb found the reverse. For the first time it detected dust, as well as gas, in the disks feeding young protostars in NGC 346, building material for stars and possibly planets.
explore: Conditions in the Small Magellanic Cloud resemble those of 'cosmic noon', the era when star formation in the universe peaked. Earlier infrared studies focused on protostars of more than about 5 to 8 solar masses, but Webb reaches down to protostars of about one tenth of the Sun's mass. The team suggests rocky planets might have formed earlier in the universe than once thought.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam captured this near-infrared view. NASA shows F444W in red, F335M in orange, F277W in cyan and F200W in blue.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the pink and orange are colours assigned to filters, not the gas's own hues.

alt: Arcs and plumes of orange and pink gas forming a boat-like shape across the centre of the frame, around the star cluster NGC 346.

caption: Part of the dwarf galaxy WLM, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Thousands of separate points and smudges fill this frame, stars and background galaxies of many colours, sizes, shapes and brightnesses. Together they make up part of the dwarf galaxy Wolf–Lundmark–Melotte, or WLM, captured by the Near-Infrared Camera on the James Webb Space Telescope.

WLM is a barred, irregular dwarf galaxy about 3 million light-years away in the constellation Cetus. A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy with far fewer stars than the Milky Way, and an irregular one lacks a tidy spiral or elliptical form.

NASA released this image to show how well Webb can resolve faint stars beyond the Milky Way. Here the galaxy is resolved into individual stars, each a separate point of light. More distant galaxies show through behind them and add to the crowd of objects in the field. The frame shows only a portion of WLM, not the whole galaxy.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam captured this in near-infrared light. NASA shows F090W (0.9 micron) in blue, F150W (1.5 micron) in cyan, F250M (2.5 micron) in yellow and F430M (4.3 micron) in red.
understand.eye: These wavelengths are longer than red light and invisible to the eye.

alt: Thousands of stars and background galaxies of various colours, sizes, shapes and brightness.

caption: The Orion Bar in the Orion Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A diagonal ridge of gas and dust runs through the lower left quarter of this Hubble image of the Orion Nebula, among clouds of varied colour, bright white foreground stars and many red, star-like points behind them. This ridge is the Orion Bar. Intense radiation from nearby hot, young stars has sculpted it.

Scientists see the Orion Bar as probably the model example of a photodissociation region, or PDR. In such a region, ultraviolet light from young, massive stars creates a warm, mostly neutral layer that sits between the fully ionized gas around the stars and the clouds where they were born. That light breaks molecules apart, strips electrons from atoms and heats the gas.

The bar is not really a single bar. It holds four distinct zones, layered like a cake, that change with distance from the massive stars much as warmth fades away from a fireplace. When this image was released in 2021, a team planned to study those zones with the James Webb Space Telescope, then scheduled to launch in October.
explore: No region of massive star formation lies closer to the Sun than the Orion Nebula. Studies of meteorites suggest the solar system formed in a similar region, so the Orion Bar is a way to learn about our own early history. Scientists also think it may resemble conditions in starburst galaxies at a time when the universe had reached roughly half of its present age.

understand.summary: A Hubble mosaic combining ACS visible-light and WFC3 infrared exposures. NASA shows F435W in blue, F555W in cyan, F775W in yellow and F139M in red.
understand.eye: The red channel comes from infrared light the eye cannot see, and many separate exposures were combined into one mosaic.

alt: A cloudy mass of gas in many colours and brightnesses with bright white stars in front and many red star-like points, crossed by a diagonal ridge in the lower left.

caption: Globular cluster Messier 92, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thousands of white stars crowd a black background in this Hubble Space Telescope image of Messier 92, or M92. It is a globular cluster, a dense, roughly round swarm of old stars held together by gravity. M92 lies about 25,000 light-years away in the constellation Hercules.

Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded the cluster through two filters. NASA ranks M92 among the brightest globular clusters in our galaxy, and its stars appear here as individual white points.

NASA released the image in 2021 alongside a preview of plans for the James Webb Space Telescope, which had not yet launched. Astronomers expected Webb's infrared instruments to reveal stars hidden even from Hubble and to pick out single stars in nearby galaxies. A team led by Daniel Weisz of the University of California, Berkeley, planned an early program on resolved stars, along with free software to help other astronomers measure them.
explore: Webb's planners hoped sharper measurements of individual stars would improve distances to nearby galaxies and so help with the open question of how fast the universe is expanding. Data from these early programs were to be shared with other astronomers right away through the Barbara A. Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS took this image through two filters. NASA shows F606W in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The colours are hues assigned to the two filters, so they are not exactly what an eye would see.

alt: Thousands of white stars on a black background.

caption: The jellyfish galaxy ESO 137-001, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Left of centre, a white-and-blue swirl trails blue filaments downward, its translucent white arms winding clockwise. This is ESO 137-001, a spiral galaxy about 220 million light-years away in the constellation Triangulum Australe, seen by Hubble in visible light. Astronomers call it a jellyfish galaxy because ribbons of young blue stars hang from its disk like tentacles.

The galaxy belongs to a cluster called Abell 3627. Hot, thin gas fills the space between a cluster's galaxies and acts like a headwind on any galaxy moving through it. That wind strips away gas and dust in a process called ram pressure stripping. Since galaxies need gas to make stars, stripping can bring star formation to an early end.

In X-rays, ESO 137-001 trails a giant tail of hot gas that stretches across 260,000 light-years, almost three times the galaxy's width. Stars seem to be forming in that tail, which puzzles researchers because stripping should have heated the gas. When the image was released in 2019, a team planned to study the tail with Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument once the telescope launched.
explore: ESO 137-001 is roughly as big as the Milky Way, with slightly less mass. Researchers planned to target star formation close to the galaxy, in the middle of the tail and near its end. Because material at the far end was stripped first, comparing these sites could show how the process changed over time.

understand.summary: A Hubble Space Telescope image in visible light. NASA has not published the filters or colour mapping for this image.
understand.eye: Hubble's visible-light view shows the blue streamers of young stars, but the giant tail of hot gas only appears in X-ray light, which the eye cannot see.

alt: A white-and-blue spiral galaxy left of centre with several blue filaments trailing downward from it.

caption: Abell 2744, or Pandora's Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Many yellow and white galaxies are scattered across black space, the biggest near the centre, with thin blue-white streaks and tiny red points sprinkled between them. This is Abell 2744, nicknamed Pandora's Cluster, formed as four smaller galaxy clusters piled together.

The cluster's mass is so great that its gravity bends light from galaxies far behind it, making them look bigger and brighter. This gravitational lensing lets astronomers study early galaxies that would otherwise be too distant to see in detail. Because Abell 2744 has been studied so thoroughly, including by Hubble, researchers can model precisely how the lens distorts background images and then work out how those galaxies would look without it.

When this image was released in 2019, a team headed by Tommaso Treu (University of California, Los Angeles) planned to use the cluster with the James Webb Space Telescope, then slated to launch in March 2021. They hoped to learn whether the first galaxies made the universe transparent to light, and how later galaxies spread heavier elements.
explore: After the big bang, the cooling universe filled with neutral hydrogen that blocked light. Scientists think the first galaxies gave off enough ultraviolet light to break up that hydrogen, ending what are called the dark ages. The team also planned deep infrared images of two fields beside the cluster to count galaxies in the very early universe.

understand.summary: A Hubble Space Telescope image. NASA has not published the filters or colour mapping for this image.
understand.eye: NASA has not published the colour mapping, so the colours should not be taken as what an eye would see, and the lensed background galaxies are too faint and distant for the eye.

scaleExtra: The cluster lies about 3.5 billion light-years away, according to NASA.
alt: Many yellow and white galaxies on a black background, the largest near the centre, with thin blue-white streaks and tiny red points of light.

caption: Star-forming region NGC 346, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A cloudy blue region stretches roughly from the upper right to the lower left corner, filled with bright white newborn stars. This is NGC 346, a giant stellar nursery about 210,000 light-years away in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring dwarf galaxy. Its infant stars are still wrapped in gas and dust.

NGC 346 stands in for the many star-forming regions that existed a few billion years after the big bang, when the universe was making stars at a furious pace. Like those early regions, it is poor in elements heavier than hydrogen and helium and holds many young, massive stars. Their ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds can tear apart star-forming clouds and disrupt the disks where planets may form.

Hubble imaged the region to identify its optically bright stars. To see stars still hidden in dust, astronomers planned at the time to use the infrared cameras on the James Webb Space Telescope, expecting a census that might reveal as many as 10,000 young stars, many under a million years old.
explore: Compared with the Small Magellanic Cloud, our galaxy holds about 25 percent more of the heavier elements. Earlier work with Spitzer and Herschel counted the massive young stars in NGC 346, those of eight solar masses or more. Webb was expected to reach stars below a solar mass, giving the full range of stellar masses in the region.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS took this image in visible and near-infrared light. NASA shows F555W in blue, a combination of F555W and F814W in green, and F814W in red.
understand.eye: Hubble recorded the optically bright stars here, while young stars still buried in dust need longer infrared wavelengths, invisible to the eye, to be found.

alt: A cloudy blue nebula stretching from upper right to lower left, filled with many bright white newborn stars.

caption: Star cluster R136 in the 30 Doradus nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A dense cluster of bright blue-white stars sits among fluffy orange and brown clouds. The cluster is R136, a massive young stellar grouping inside the 30 Doradus nebula, also called the Tarantula Nebula. It lies about 170,000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, in the constellation Dorado.

30 Doradus is a turbulent region where stars are being born. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded it through several filters, and the colours carry meaning. Blue comes from the hottest, most massive stars, green from glowing oxygen, and red from fluorescing hydrogen.

Because it is close by, this stellar nursery gives astronomers insight into the life cycle of stars, and it hints at how star clusters may have come together in the early universe. A nebula like this is a cloud of gas and dust where new stars form, and the young stars in turn light up the gas around them.
explore: Hubble collected the data between 20 and 27 October 2009, with exposure times of 11.7 hours for the ultraviolet-visible channel and 2.6 hours for the infrared channel of Wide Field Camera 3.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 took this image. NASA shows F336W and F438W in blue, F555W in green, F814W in red, and the hydrogen-alpha filter F656N in orange-red.
understand.eye: Exposures adding up to many hours gather far more light than the eye can, and some of the data comes from ultraviolet light, which the eye cannot see.

alt: A dense cluster of bright blue-white stars surrounded by fluffy orange and brown clouds.

caption: The Bullseye galaxy LEDA 1313424, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A large galaxy sits at the centre with a much smaller one just to its left, against black space dotted with distant galaxies and a few foreground stars. The big one is LEDA 1313424, nicknamed the Bullseye, a collisional ring galaxy about 567 million light-years away in Pisces. Its nine rings are six more than any other known galaxy has.

Hubble's sharp imaging confirmed eight of the rings, many of them piled up near the centre, and the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii added the ninth. The two telescopes also showed which galaxy caused them. The small blue dwarf on the left plunged through the Bullseye's core about 50 million years ago, sending out rings like ripples from a pebble dropped in a pond.

Stars mostly kept to their orbits, but groups of them piled up into rings, while gas was carried outward and formed new stars. The rings appear to have spread outward almost exactly as long-standing models predicted. A thin trail of gas still links the two galaxies, now 130,000 light-years apart.
explore: The Bullseye is about 250,000 light-years across, almost two and a half times the size of the Milky Way. The team suspects a 10th ring once existed but has faded. Hubble sees the galaxy at a slight angle, and from directly above the rings would look circular, bunched near the centre and spaced more widely farther out.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS took this image. NASA shows F475W in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The cyan and orange are hues assigned to two filters, and the researchers say pinning down the rings bunched near the centre would have been impossible without Hubble's sharp vision.

alt: A large galaxy at centre with a much smaller galaxy to its immediate left, on a black background dotted with galaxies and a few stars.

caption: Giant galaxy M87 and its jet, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
captureDate: December 2005 - March 2006 and November 2016 to July 2017
story: A fuzzy white glow fades gradually outward from a bright point at its centre, and a wavy blue-white jet reaches from that core toward the upper right. This is M87, a giant elliptical galaxy about 53 million light-years away in Virgo, home to several trillion stars and thousands of globular star clusters.

The jet is a 3,000-light-year-long stream of plasma launched by the galaxy's central black hole of 6.5 billion solar masses. It seems to make stars erupt along its path. These eruptions are novae, and Hubble found twice as many of them near the jet as elsewhere in the galaxy during a nine-month survey.

A nova happens in a pair of stars where a swollen, ageing star spills hydrogen onto a white dwarf until that layer explodes. The white dwarf survives and the cycle starts again. Researchers do not know why the jet boosts the number of novae. It might push hydrogen onto the white dwarfs, or act on them through the pressure of its light.
explore: Finding the novae meant revisiting M87 every five days, and adding up the images produced the deepest views of M87 ever taken. Hubble found 94 novae in the third of the galaxy its camera covers. Ground-based telescopes cannot pick out novae near the core, because the region around the black hole is too bright.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3/UVIS took this image through two filters. NASA shows F275W in cyan and F606W in orange.
understand.eye: The image combines many separate exposures, and the colours are hues assigned to two filters rather than what an eye would see.

alt: A fuzzy white elliptical galaxy with a bright point at its centre and a wavy blue-white jet extending to the upper right.

caption: Interacting galaxy AM 1054-325, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright milky-white core sits at the centre of an S-shaped galaxy, wrapped by twin arms of blue stars. One arm looks especially stretched out and is strung with bright, young, whitish star clusters. This is AM 1054-325, about 173 million light-years away in the constellation Antlia.

The galaxy was once a normal pancake-shaped spiral. The gravity of a neighbouring galaxy has stretched it, drawing out a tidal tail where newborn star clusters have formed for thousands of light-years like a string of pearls. Each one forms when a knot of gas collapses under its own gravity to make about 1 million stars.

AM 1054-325 is one of 12 interacting galaxies in a Hubble study that found 425 young clusters in their tails. The clusters are only 10 million years old, and their future is uncertain. They may stay intact and become globular clusters, disperse into a halo around their galaxy, or drift off as wandering stars between galaxies.
explore: Collisions jostle dusty clouds of molecular hydrogen that might otherwise have stayed inert, compressing the gas until it bursts into star formation. Star birth of this kind may have been more frequent long ago, when galaxies collided more often, so nearby examples like this one work as laboratories for studying the distant past.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's WFPC2 and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F336W in magenta, F435W in cyan, F606W in green and F814W in red.
understand.eye: Hubble's sensitivity to ultraviolet light helps pick out the young star clusters, and ultraviolet light is invisible to the eye.

alt: An S-shaped galaxy with a bright milky-white core and two arms of blue stars, one arm stretched out and dotted with bright whitish star clusters.

caption: Dwarf irregular galaxy UGC 8091, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A dense spread of blue and orange stars fills most of the frame, with patches of blue toward the middle and distant galaxies scattered across the dark background. This is UGC 8091, a dwarf galaxy of about a billion stars, approximately 7 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. NASA likens it to a sparkling snow globe.

UGC 8091 counts as an irregular galaxy because it has no orderly spiral or elliptical shape, and its stars look more like a tangle of string lights. Some irregular galaxies may have been scrambled by violent activity inside them, while others took shape through encounters with neighbouring galaxies, so the class comes in many sizes and forms.

The red patches are likely hydrogen gas glowing because light from hot, energetic stars has excited it. The other sparkles are a mix of older stars. The observing programs behind the image looked at the part dwarf galaxies played, billions of years ago, in heating up again the hydrogen that cooled as the young universe expanded.
explore: Twelve filters were combined for the image, covering light from the mid-ultraviolet to the red end of the visible spectrum. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys gathered the data between 2006 and 2021. Astronomers are also studying what dwarf galaxies and their stars are made of, to trace links between such ancient galaxies and modern ones like the Milky Way.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's WFC3 and ACS cameras. NASA shows F218N, F225W and F275W in purple, F336W, F373N and F487N in blue, F475W and F502N in cyan, F475W in green, F814W in orange, and F656N, F657N, F110W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Part of the light is ultraviolet, which the eye cannot see, and the picture combines exposures gathered over many years.

alt: A dense collection of blue and orange stars forming an irregular galaxy, with blue patches in the centre and background galaxies on a dark sky.

caption: The Peekaboo dwarf galaxy HIPASS J1131–31, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A large bright star sits in the middle with four long rays spreading in an X, and between the rays on the right lies a small blue, peanut-shaped galaxy with a few bright spots. That little galaxy is HIPASS J1131–31, nicknamed Peekaboo, about 22 million light-years away in Hydra. The glaring star, TYC 7215-199-1, belongs to our own galaxy.

The foreground star moves quickly across the sky. A century ago it would have sat directly in front of the galaxy, which could not have been detected then. Peekaboo has emerged from behind it only in the past 50 to 100 years.

Hubble resolved about 60 stars in the galaxy, and nearly every one seems to be no more than a few billion years old. That is very unusual nearby, where galaxies typically hold ancient stars. Peekaboo is also extremely poor in elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, so it gives astronomers a close look at conditions usually found only in the distant, early universe.
explore: The galaxy is only 1,200 light-years across. It was first detected more than 20 years ago as a patch of cold hydrogen by the Parkes radio telescope Murriyang in Australia. The Southern African Large Telescope measured its metal content, and the team plans further study with Hubble and Webb.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS took this image. NASA shows F606W in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The four long rays around the bright star are an effect of the telescope's optics, not part of the star itself, and the colours are hues assigned to two filters.

alt: A bright star with four long rays in an X shape, with a small blue peanut-shaped galaxy between the rays on the right, among smaller stars and orange background galaxies.

caption: Hickson Compact Group 40, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Five galaxies crowd together in this Hubble image of Hickson Compact Group 40, released to mark the telescope's 32nd birthday. The group holds three spiral galaxies, an elliptical galaxy and a lens-shaped lenticular galaxy, about 300 million light-years away in the direction of Hydra.

The whole group could fit inside a region less than twice the diameter of the Milky Way's stellar disk. Such tight groupings occur in the hearts of huge galaxy clusters, but these galaxies sit isolated in their own patch of the universe. One possible explanation is a large amount of dark matter. Moving through a shared cloud of it, the galaxies would feel a drag from its gravity, lose energy and fall together.

In about 1 billion years they are expected to collide and merge into a giant elliptical galaxy. Nearly every member has a compact radio source at its core, which could point to supermassive black holes, and X-ray observations reveal plenty of hot gas between the galaxies, a sign of their gravitational interaction.
explore: Sky surveys have catalogued over 100 compact groups like this, and few are as densely packed as Hickson Compact Group 40. Such tight groups may have been more common in the early universe, where they may have fuelled quasars. Paul Hickson of the University of British Columbia rediscovered the group while browsing Halton Arp's 1966 collection of peculiar galaxies.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 took this image. NASA shows F475W in blue, F606W in green, and F814W and F665N in red.
understand.eye: The colours are hues assigned to four filters, including the narrow F665N, so they are not exactly what an eye would see.

alt: Five galaxies close together: a tilted spiral at upper left, a large elliptical just above centre, and three touching galaxies toward the lower right.

caption: Interacting galaxies Arp 143, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: On the right, a distorted spiral galaxy glitters with a triangle of new stars, and on the left sits a plainer companion. The pair is Arp 143, about 191 million light-years away in Lynx. The busy one is NGC 2445, and its partner is NGC 2444.

Astronomers suggest the two galaxies passed through each other in a head-on collision, setting off a burst of star birth in gas-rich NGC 2445, where thousands of stars are forming. Head-on collisions can make rings of new stars, but here NGC 2444 still holds its partner in a gravitational grip, pulling away gas and bending the ring into a triangle.

NGC 2444 has also drawn out streamers of young, blue stars that seem to form a bridge between the two galaxies. They appear to be among the first in a wave of star formation that moved inward. Researchers estimate these stars formed some 50 million to 100 million years ago, while nearer the centre of NGC 2445 the newest stars are just 1 million to 2 million years old.
explore: Most of the bright blue clumps are groups of stars, while the pink blobs are huge, young clusters still wrapped in dust and gas. NGC 2444 has been stretched into an odd shape too. It holds only old stars and makes no new ones, because it lost its gas long before this encounter.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F475W in blue, F606W in green, and F814W and F665N in red.
understand.eye: The colours are hues assigned to several filters, including the narrow F665N, and Hubble's sharpness picks out some individual stars in NGC 2445, the brightest and most massive in the galaxy.

alt: Two interacting galaxies, a glittering distorted spiral with a triangle of star formation on the right and a plainer companion on the left.

caption: The Southern Crab Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A colourful hourglass shape spreads out from a bright white star, with a glowing figure eight at its centre. This is the Southern Crab Nebula, officially Hen 2-104, about 10,700 light-years away in the southern constellation Centaurus. Hubble took the image to mark its 29th launch anniversary.

The nebula has two nested hourglasses, shaped by a pair of stars orbiting each other, an ageing red giant and a white dwarf. As the giant sheds its outer layers, the white dwarf's gravity pulls in some of that material, so both stars sit inside a flat disk of gas. The disk pinches the outflow so gas escapes only above and below it.

The bubbles are brightest at their edges, which makes them look like crab legs. These are likely where the outflow strikes surrounding gas and dust. The outer structure may be only thousands of years old, and the inner hourglass is more recent. Eventually the red giant will collapse into a white dwarf, and the two white dwarfs will light up a planetary nebula.
explore: First reported in the late 1960s, the object was at first taken for an ordinary star. Astronomers using ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile photographed a roughly crab-shaped nebula in 1989, and Hubble revealed the nested structures in 1999. The colours trace glowing gases, with red marking sulfur and blue marking oxygen.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 took this image through narrow filters. NASA shows F502N in blue, F656N in orange, F658N in green and F673N in red.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate light from individual glowing gases, and the colours are assigned to bring out the nebula's chemistry rather than to match what an eye would see.

alt: A colourful hourglass-shaped nebula with a bright white star and a glowing figure eight at its centre.

caption: Galaxy cluster Abell S1063, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A soft blue haze spreads among countless galaxies in the cluster Abell S1063, about 4 billion light-years away in the constellation Grus. The haze is intracluster light, the glow of stars that have been thrown out of their galaxies.

Those stars no longer belong to any galaxy. Torn loose during interactions between galaxies, they now follow the gravity of the cluster as a whole, the same gravity that governs the cluster's invisible dark matter. Because they trace the same pull, the faint glow works as a map of where the dark matter lies.

A study using Hubble Frontier Fields images of six massive galaxy clusters found that intracluster light matched the clusters' mass maps better than X-ray emission did. The method needs only deep imaging rather than slower spectroscopy, so many more clusters could be studied in less time. In the original Frontier Fields work, the glow was a nuisance that partly hid distant galaxies behind the clusters.
explore: Mireia Montes (University of New South Wales) and Ignacio Trujillo (Canary Islands Institute of Astronomy) carried out the work. They compared shapes using a measure called the Modified Hausdorff Distance. Trujillo hoped to try the same approach on single galaxies, using the stars in their halos.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras in visible and near-infrared light. NASA shows F435W and F606W in blue, F814W and F105W in green, and F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Intracluster light is a faint glow that Hubble's sensitivity picks out, and part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.

alt: Many galaxies of a massive cluster embedded in a soft blue haze.

caption: Galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1-2403, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Among the bright member galaxies of MACS J0416.1-2403 lies a soft glow of intracluster light, made by stars that belong to no single galaxy. The cluster is about 4 billion light-years away in the constellation Eridanus.

Those stars were scattered through the cluster long ago, when its gravity tore apart their home galaxies. Over time they lined up with the gravity of the cluster as a whole. Invisible dark matter dominates that gravitational field, so the faint starlight traces where the dark matter is.

Astronomers tested the idea on Hubble Frontier Fields images of six massive clusters. They found the glow matched the clusters' mass maps more closely than X-ray light did, since X-rays mark where groups of galaxies collide rather than the underlying structure. The approach relies only on deep images, without slower spectroscopy, so it could be applied to many more clusters and might eventually help reveal what dark matter is.
explore: The Frontier Fields program used the gravity of galaxy clusters as a natural magnifying glass to study very distant galaxies behind them, and in that work the intracluster light was a nuisance. The researchers hoped to apply the method with future telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope and WFIRST.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras in visible and near-infrared light. NASA shows F435W and F606W in blue, F814W and F105W in green, and F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: The faint glow of these scattered stars is picked out by Hubble's sensitivity, and part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.

alt: Bright galaxies of a massive cluster surrounded by a faint, soft glow.

caption: A region of the Andromeda Galaxy and its star clusters, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble close-up shows a region of the Andromeda galaxy, M31, along with some of its star clusters. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy and the nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away in the constellation Andromeda.

The view comes from the Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Treasury, or PHAT, a survey of the galaxy's disk. Nearly 8,000 images of 117 million stars were taken in near-ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light, and assembled into 414 mosaic photographs.

Using 2,753 young, blue star clusters found in those images, astronomers measured what share of a cluster's stars form at each mass. Andromeda and the Milky Way turned out to have a similar share of newborn stars by mass, and the distribution was very similar from cluster to cluster. The brightest, most massive stars were 25 percent less common than earlier research had predicted.
explore: About 30,000 volunteers helped find the clusters through the Andromeda Project, hosted by Zooniverse. Over 25 days they made 1.82 million image classifications, raising the number of known clusters in the survey region by a factor of six. The clusters are between 4 million and 24 million years old.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F336W in blue, F475W in green, F814W in yellow and F160W in red.
understand.eye: The image includes near-ultraviolet and near-infrared light, both invisible to the eye, and Hubble picks out individual stars in another galaxy.

alt: A close-up of a region of the Andromeda galaxy and its star clusters.

caption: Elliptical galaxy M60, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble Space Telescope image shows the massive elliptical galaxy M60, with part of the faint, bluish spiral galaxy NGC 4647 peeking into the upper right corner. M60 lies about 50 million light-years away inside the Virgo Cluster, an immense gathering of 2,500 galaxies.

An elliptical galaxy is a rounded collection of stars without spiral arms. At its heart M60 holds a monster black hole of 4.5 billion solar masses, which outweighs the Milky Way's central black hole by a factor of more than 1,000.

Close to M60 sits a tiny companion, the ultracompact dwarf galaxy M60-UCD1, which packs 140 million stars into a diameter of about 300 light-years. Using Hubble and the Gemini North telescope, astronomers found that it too holds a supermassive black hole, amounting to 15 percent of its mass. A possible explanation is that M60-UCD1 began as a large galaxy and passed close to the centre of M60 and lost its outer stars and dark matter to it. It may eventually merge with the core of M60.
explore: M60-UCD1 is the densest galaxy ever seen. Anyone living inside it would see at least 1 million stars with the naked eye, compared with the 4,000 visible from Earth. The finding suggests some dwarf galaxies may be the stripped remains of larger galaxies rather than small star systems that formed on their own.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 cameras. NASA shows F475W and F555W in blue, a blend of F475W, F555W, F850LP and F814W in green, and F850LP and F814W in red.
understand.eye: The colours are hues assigned to several filters, including near-infrared ones that record light the eye cannot see.

alt: A large elliptical galaxy with part of a faint bluish spiral galaxy in the upper right corner.

caption: Galaxy cluster IRC 0218, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows IRC 0218, a distant cluster of galaxies in the constellation Eridanus. One of its brightest members is a monster elliptical galaxy, seen as it looked 9.6 billion years ago, that acts as a natural magnifying glass. When it was found, it was the most distant lensing galaxy known, beating the previous record holder by 200 million years.

Its gravity bends, magnifies and distorts light from a tiny spiral galaxy behind it, which is going through a rapid burst of star formation. Light from that background galaxy took 10.7 billion years to reach us. Hubble pictures in blue wavelengths showed a blue, eyebrow-shaped object beside a smeared blue dot around the big elliptical, the stretched images of the farther galaxy.

By gauging how strongly the lens bends light, astronomers weighed the elliptical at 180 billion times the Sun's mass, a heavyweight for its era. Surprisingly, it holds little dark matter compared with closer elliptical galaxies. The team suspects it will keep growing over the next 9 billion years by swallowing neighbouring galaxies.
explore: Kim-Vy Tran of Texas A&M University spotted the lens while studying star formation in distant clusters. Spectra from the W.M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii showed hot hydrogen gas, a sign of star birth, apparently coming from an old galaxy that had stopped forming stars long ago. The young stars turned out to lie much farther away, behind the elliptical.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F475W in blue, F814W in green, and F105W, F125W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: The image combines 3.3 hours of exposure and includes near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.

alt: Galaxies of the distant cluster IRC 0218.

caption: Hubble Ultra Deep Field 2014, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thousands of galaxies spread across the dark backdrop of space in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field 2014, a small section of sky in the southern constellation Fornax. The image holds roughly 10,000 galaxies, and the most distant are seen as they were only a few hundred million years after the big bang.

Astronomers had already studied this field in visible and near-infrared light. The 2014 version adds ultraviolet, combining the full range of colours available to Hubble. Exposures from 2002 to 2012, made with two Hubble cameras (ACS and WFC3), went into it, using 841 orbits of observing time.

The hottest, largest and youngest stars give off ultraviolet light, so it shows which galaxies are forming stars and where. That fills a gap for the period, between about 5 billion and 10 billion light-years away, when most of the universe's stars were born. Because Earth's atmosphere blocks most ultraviolet light, the work needs a telescope in space.
explore: Researchers describe the study behind it, called Ultraviolet Coverage of the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, as the missing link in star formation. Principal investigator Harry Teplitz of Caltech compared the earlier gap to studying family histories without knowing about the grade-school children. The ultraviolet data were expected to be combined with infrared data from the James Webb Space Telescope.

understand.summary: A composite of 13 filters from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras, spanning ultraviolet to near-infrared. NASA shows the ultraviolet and blue-visible filters (F150LP, F225W, F275W, F336W, F435W and F606W) in blue, F775W, F814W, F850LP and F105W in green, and F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: The exposures add up to about 600 hours and include ultraviolet and infrared light that the eye cannot see, revealing galaxies far beyond its reach.

alt: Thousands of galaxies spread across dark space.

caption: Planetary nebula NGC 5189, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright golden ring twists and tilts through the frame among bluish lobes of knotty, filament-laced gas. This is NGC 5189, a planetary nebula about 3,000 light-years away in the constellation Musca, whose intricate shape NASA likened to a glass-blown holiday ornament wrapped in a glowing ribbon.

A planetary nebula marks the last, short phase of life for a medium-sized star like the Sun. As the dying star burns the last fuel in its core, it throws off much of its outer envelope. Radiation from the remaining star heats that material until it glows, and because the star sheds mass unevenly in time and direction, the clouds take on complex shapes.

NGC 5189 has two nested structures, tilted relative to each other and expanding in different directions. A companion star orbiting the central star could explain this pattern, though no visible candidate has been found. The central remnant is now a white dwarf. The golden ring is made of radial filaments and cometary knots, usually shaped by ionizing radiation and stellar winds.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded the nebula in filters tuned to the colours of glowing sulfur, hydrogen and oxygen atoms, while broad filters in visible and near-infrared light captured the colours of the stars. The total exposure time was 7 hours.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 took this image. NASA shows F502N (oxygen) in cyan, F657N (hydrogen-alpha and nitrogen) in orange, F673N (sulfur) in green, F606W in blue and F814W in yellow.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of individual elements, and the colours are assigned to separate them rather than to match what an eye would see.

alt: A planetary nebula with bluish lobes of knotty, filamentary gas and a bright golden ring twisting through it.

caption: Galaxy cluster MACS J1149+2223, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the massive galaxy cluster MACS J1149+2223, about 5.3 billion light-years away in the constellation Leo. Its gravity works as a natural lens, and behind it astronomers found a galaxy that, when announced in 2012, could have been the farthest ever observed.

Gravitational lensing, predicted by Albert Einstein a century ago, happens when the gravity of foreground objects warps and magnifies light from objects behind them. This cluster brightened the remote galaxy some 15 times, bringing it into view. Its light first shone when the universe was just 500 million years old and travelled approximately 13.2 billion light-years to reach Hubble and NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope.

The galaxy is small and compact, holding only about one percent as much mass as the Milky Way, and astronomers think it was less than 200 million years old when its light set out. It dates from the era when the universe began to emerge from the cosmic dark ages, which the first galaxies likely helped to end.
explore: Hubble detected the galaxy in four visible and infrared bands for the CLASH cluster lensing survey, and Spitzer added a fifth, longer-wavelength band. Earlier candidates of this age had been seen in only one. Astronomers expected it to be a prime target for the James Webb Space Telescope, which was then scheduled for launch in 2018.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F435W, F475W and F555W in blue, F606W, F625W and F775W in green, and F814W, F850LP, F105W, F110W, F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: The total exposure time was 11.3 hours, and part of the light is infrared, which the eye cannot see.

alt: Galaxies of the massive cluster MACS J1149+2223.

caption: Globular cluster NGC 1846, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view shows a spherical swarm of hundreds of thousands of stars. Ageing bright stars glow in intense red and blue, while most of the middle-aged stars, several billion years old, look whitish. This is NGC 1846, a globular cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud's outer halo. That neighbouring dwarf galaxy of the Milky Way is visible from the southern hemisphere.

Near the bottom centre sits a faint green bubble that seems out of place. It is a planetary nebula, the aftermath of a star's death, and the burned-out central star shows inside it. Nobody is sure whether the bubble belongs to the cluster or just happens to sit in the same direction, though measurements of the motions of the cluster stars and the nebula's central star suggest it might be a member.
Many distant background galaxies of varied shapes and structures are scattered around the cluster. Seen toward the constellation Dorado, NGC 1846 is roughly 160,000 light-years away.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took the image in January 2006, using filters that isolate blue, green and infrared starlight. A globular cluster is a tightly bound, roughly spherical group of old stars held together by its own gravity.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS took this image. NASA shows F435W in blue, F555W in green and F814W in red.
understand.eye: The exposure totals 34 minutes and includes near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.

alt: A spherical cluster of red, blue and whitish stars, with a faint green bubble near the bottom centre and distant galaxies scattered around.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 5584, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Blue light from young stars traces the graceful spiral arms of NGC 5584, and thin dark dust lanes seem to flow out from its yellowish core, where older stars live. The reddish dots scattered across the frame are mostly background galaxies. NGC 5584 lies about 72 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

Its stars include pulsating Cepheid variables, and it recently hosted a Type Ia supernova, a special class of exploding star. A Cepheid pulsates at a rate closely tied to its true brightness, which makes it a good distance marker for relatively nearby galaxies. Type Ia supernovae all flare with the same brightness and can be seen much farther away.

Comparing the two kinds of star in the same galaxy lets astronomers calibrate supernovae in distant galaxies and work out how far away those galaxies are. NGC 5584 was one of eight galaxies used in this way, with more than 600 Cepheids analysed in total, 250 of them here. The work measured how fast the universe is expanding today with an uncertainty of just 3.3 percent.
explore: The team, led by Adam Riess of the Space Telescope Science Institute and Johns Hopkins University, found an expansion rate of 73.8 kilometers per second per megaparsec. That ruled out the idea that we live near the centre of a huge bubble of relatively empty space, an alternative explanation for the apparent acceleration usually attributed to dark energy.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 took this image in visible light. NASA shows F350LP in white, F555W in blue and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The exposures add up to 20.8 hours, gathering far more light than the eye could, enough to pick out individual pulsating stars in another galaxy.

alt: A spiral galaxy with blue spiral arms, thin dark dust lanes and a yellowish core, with reddish dots of background galaxies scattered around.

caption: Barred spiral galaxy NGC 6217, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image of the barred spiral galaxy NGC 6217 was the first astronomical picture made with the Advanced Camera for Surveys after its repair. Its distance is 60 million light-years, and it sits in the far northern sky.

Astronauts restored the camera during the STS-125 servicing mission in May 2009, which upgraded the Hubble Space Telescope, and the galaxy was photographed in June and July as part of the camera's first tests and calibration. On the same mission, astronauts installed two new instruments, Wide Field Camera 3 and the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, and repaired the Advanced Camera for Surveys and the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph at the circuit board level.

Before the servicing mission, only three unique instrument channels still worked. Afterward there were 13, and NASA declared Hubble a fully rejuvenated observatory, more sensitive and able to finish observations in a fraction of the time older instruments needed. A barred spiral like NGC 6217 has a bar-shaped band of stars across its centre, with spiral arms extending from it.
explore: At the time, NASA expected the upgraded telescope to study everything from Kuiper Belt objects at the edge of the solar system to the atmospheres of planets around other stars, and to make the deepest near-infrared image of the universe yet attempted.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS took this image. NASA shows F814W and the hydrogen-alpha filter F658N in red, F625W in green and F435W in blue.
understand.eye: The exposures total 3.0 hours, gathering far more light than the eye could from a galaxy this far away.

alt: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 6217.
